title: The Merry Wives of Windsor
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — Windsor. Before Page's house
openingText: Sir Hugh Evans and Justice Shallow arrive at Windsor with a complaint against Sir John Falstaff for poaching deer and breaking into Shallow's lodge.
about:
Sir John Falstaff arrives in Windsor short of money and writes identical love letters to Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, intending to seduce both wives and live off their husbands' purses. The wives compare letters within an hour, are united in disgust, and decide to take their revenge by leading him through a series of humiliating practical jokes. Falstaff is folded into a buck-basket of dirty laundry and dumped in the Thames. He is dressed as the fat woman of Brentford and beaten through the streets. He is finally lured to Herne's Oak at midnight in deer antlers and pinched and burned by Windsor children dressed as fairies. He gives up.

In the meantime, three suitors compete for the Pages' young daughter Anne: the foolish Justice Shallow's nephew Slender, the volatile French doctor Caius, and the gentleman she actually loves, Fenton. The parents quarrel about which of the two unwanted suitors to force her into. At the fairy ambush in Windsor Park, Anne elopes with Fenton in the confusion, and Slender and Caius each find themselves married to a boy in disguise. Master Ford, who has spent the play disguised as 'Master Brook' to test his wife's loyalty, is taught a lesson about jealousy.

Shakespeare wrote The Merry Wives of Windsor around 1597, very probably on commission. The standard story is that Queen Elizabeth, having loved Falstaff in the Henry IV plays, asked for a play of 'Falstaff in love.' Shakespeare gave her one. The result is his only comedy set in contemporary, middle-class English life — a play of suburb wives, country justices, a French doctor, a Welsh parson, a German horse-thief subplot, and the fat knight of the histories transplanted into the wrong century.

angleCards.title: The wives.
angleCards.text: The play is the rare Shakespeare comedy with two married women at its centre, both clever, both faithful, both running the plot. Mistress Ford and Mistress Page are the heroes.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the play as the wives' play: how Mistress Ford and Mistress Page handle Falstaff, how they handle their husbands, and how the comedy gives them the upper hand all five acts.

angleCards.title: Falstaff out of his element.
angleCards.text: The Falstaff of the Henry IV plays was a tavern philosopher with a court connection. The Falstaff of Merry Wives is a fortune-hunter chasing tradesmen's wives in a country town. Read the demotion. It is part of the joke.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Windsor Falstaff with the Eastcheap Falstaff in mind, and see what Shakespeare does — and refuses to do — with his most famous character in a wholly different setting.

angleCards.title: Master Ford's jealousy.
angleCards.text: Ford spends most of the play disguised as 'Master Brook,' paying Falstaff to seduce his own wife so that he can catch them in the act. The play makes serious comedy of his suspicion and asks where it comes from.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the Master Ford / Master Brook subplot as Shakespeare's comic study of jealousy — how Ford manufactures the very evidence he fears, and what is finally done to cure him.

angleCards.title: Windsor in 1597.
angleCards.text: Merry Wives is Shakespeare's only comedy set in contemporary England, full of local references, English mid-sized-town life, and the kind of jokes the original audience could match against streets they knew.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Merry Wives as Shakespeare's English-suburb comedy — the only play of his set in his own time and his own country — and notice what the choice lets him do.

cast.name: Sir John Falstaff
cast.description: The Falstaff of the Henry IV plays, transplanted to a Berkshire market town and short of money. He writes identical love letters to two married women and is humiliated three times in escalating set-pieces by both of them at once.

cast.name: Mistress Page
cast.description: A respectable Windsor wife, mother to Anne and William, and one half of the duo who orchestrate Falstaff's punishment. Clever, decisive, and protective of her daughter against her husband's preferred suitor.

cast.name: Mistress Ford
cast.description: Mistress Page's closest friend and Falstaff's other intended victim. Married to the jealous Master Ford and forced to manage both the prank on Falstaff and the gradual cure of her husband's suspicion.

cast.name: Master Ford
cast.description: A Windsor citizen consumed by suspicion of his wife. He spends most of the play disguised as 'Master Brook' to bribe Falstaff into providing the evidence of an affair he is sure must exist. He receives his cure at Herne's Oak.

cast.name: Master Page
cast.description: Mistress Page's good-natured husband, untroubled by Falstaff's letters and quietly opposed to his daughter's match with the gentleman she loves. He prefers the foolish Slender as a son-in-law.

cast.name: Anne Page
cast.description: The Pages' young daughter, courted by Slender, Doctor Caius, and Master Fenton. She loves Fenton. The play gives her a single-mindedness her parents do not yet appreciate, and lets her elope at the fairy masque.

acclaim.quote: It is said to have been written at the express command of Queen Elizabeth, who was so much delighted with the character of Falstaff in the two parts of Henry IV that she wished to see him exhibited once more, and in love.
acclaim.context: Some Account of the Life of Mr William Shakespear, 1709

acclaim.quote: The Merry Wives of Windsor is no doubt a very amusing play, with a great deal of humour, character, and nature in it.

whyItMatters.title: The Only Suburb Comedy
whyItMatters.body: The Merry Wives of Windsor is the only Shakespeare comedy set in contemporary England. Every other comedy is in Illyria, in Athens, in the forest of Arden, in Padua, in Ephesus — places the audience would never visit, where the rules of social life could be loosened or invented. Merry Wives is in Windsor, where the Globe's first audience could find every street if they liked. Falstaff drinks at the Garter Inn, which existed; the children pinch him under Herne's Oak, which existed; the wives go shopping in the same town the audience went shopping in. The result is Shakespeare's most domestically observed comedy: real money problems, real marriage problems, two clever wives running a small intelligent revenge on a man who tried to extract money from them through their bedrooms. The play has been more popular on the English stage than almost any other Shakespeare comedy, for what is presumably an obvious reason: an English audience could see itself in it without much translation.

whyItMatters.title: The Wives Win
whyItMatters.body: Almost no other Shakespeare comedy puts two married women at the centre and lets them run the plot. Merry Wives does. From the moment Mistress Page and Mistress Ford compare Falstaff's identical letters in Act 2 they are in charge. They invent the buck-basket trick. They invent the witch of Brentford. They invent the fairy masque. Their husbands either don't know what is happening (Master Page) or are running their own less competent parallel plot (Master Ford). Even Anne Page's elopement is, in its way, a small daughter's continuation of the family's pattern: take the choice into your own hands and surprise the men. The play has been read in modern criticism as a study of a community of women managing what their husbands cannot, and it is one of the few places in the comic canon where the joke about men is the central joke, told by the women, and they get to walk offstage at the end having won every round of it.

whyItMatters.title: Falstaff in the Wrong Play
whyItMatters.body: Shakespeare invented Falstaff in Henry IV, Part 1 as a tavern philosopher with a court connection, a soldier's commission, and a prince's friendship. Merry Wives takes him out of all of that and drops him in a small English market town with empty pockets and tradesmen's wives to chase. Critics have argued for centuries whether this is the same Falstaff, or whether Shakespeare wrote a comic stranger who happens to share the name. Tradition has it that Queen Elizabeth requested 'Falstaff in love' after enjoying him in the histories; the result is Falstaff trying to be in love and failing comprehensively. He still tells lies; he is still huge; he is still inexhaustibly verbal. But the wisdom of Eastcheap is gone. He gets dumped in the river. He gets dressed as a woman and beaten. He gets put in antlers and pinched by children. The play is a holiday from the histories and a study of what its character looks like outside the world that made him meaningful. Whether the price is worth paying is what audiences for four centuries have been arguing about.
